analysis: The closest response retains substantial biology and neuroscience alongside psychology: evolution, cellular/molecular biology, physiology, pharmacology, neurobiology, perception, cognition, development and mental health. Evolution replaces general philosophy, laboratory biology replaces regional anatomy and research methods replaces philosophy of emotion, strengthening the defining experimental and biological substance.

The cognitive-data option retains brain, cognition, language and quantitative methods but replaces robotics and persuasion with life-science foundations and cell biology. Computer vision, artificial networks and decision/optimisation models are described as computational complements, not biological neural mechanisms. The biological/disease option retains its coherent cellular, genetic, physiological, pharmacological, laboratory and disease focus, with a bounded label rather than implying that all biomedical work is specialised molecular neuroscience.

Every selected course contribution was reconsidered from available profile or description evidence. Description-only perception/action and psycholinguistics receive full consideration. Sixteen bounded matches use identifiable subject or method content. Evolution is placed with Evolution/Behaviour, meta-analysis with the literature review, and actual research methods with introductory research/statistics. Removed a philosophical-emotion/internal-regulation pairing and a meta-analysis/compulsory-internship pairing; developmental psychology is explicitly a partial relationship to an embryological and neural-development course.

The three original offering conflicts are repaired within current terms. Psycholinguistics has only its first Spring offering in the current plan and is placed there after Brain and Behavior, concurrently with Neurobiology; a stricter advisory order was tested and infeasible, but is not a formal prerequisite. Neurobiology precedes Higher Order Functions; methods/data foundations precede later analysis. All schedules pass numerical and formal gates, every pair meets thirty EC each way, and optional research is parallel to the actual project outside scheduled credits.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.contribution: Academic writing, literature evaluation, civic collaboration and reflective practice provide the first-year common foundation.

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.contribution: develops empirical design, measurement, sampling, statistics and a student data-collection project as foundations for experimental brain/behaviour inquiry

DISARIN211.name: Decision-making in AI
DISARIN211.contribution: develops probability, Bayesian inference and sequential decisions under uncertainty as computational tools for modelling decisions; it does not itself establish biological decision mechanisms

DISARIN212.name: Logic & Discrete Mathematics
DISARIN212.contribution: develops logic, proof, discrete structures and formal modelling as mathematical foundations for computational analysis

DISARIN311.name: Optimization Methods in AI
DISARIN311.contribution: develops algorithmic search and continuous/discrete optimisation, including implementation and experimental evaluation, as tools for computational modelling

DISCOMP311.name: Algorithms & Data Structures
DISCOMP311.contribution: develops algorithm design, complexity and data structures for implementing and evaluating computational analysis efficiently

DISDATA111.name: Introduction to Data Science
DISDATA111.contribution: develops data cleaning, transformation, visualisation and applied research in R for empirical biological and behavioural data

DISDATA211.name: Machine Learning
DISDATA211.contribution: develops regression, classification, model evaluation and statistical prediction on real data, complementing experimental analysis

DISDATA212.name: Image Processing & Computer Vision
DISDATA212.contribution: develops digital-image processing, segmentation, feature detection and recognition in Python as computational counterparts to studying visual information processing

DISDATA311.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
DISDATA311.contribution: develops artificial neural-network theory, model training and evaluation for image, text and time-series prediction; this computational contribution is distinguished from biological neural mechanisms

DISGATE101.name: Introduction to Programming
DISGATE101.contribution: develops Python programming, structured problem solving and program testing for implementing experimental tasks and data workflows

DISGATE102.name: Mathematical Methods
DISGATE102.contribution: develops calculus, differential equations and dynamic modelling as mathematical tools for quantitative biological and computational inquiry

DISMATH314.name: Probability & Statistics
DISMATH314.contribution: develops probability distributions, inference, likelihood, Bayesian reasoning and simulation as a rigorous statistical complement to biomedical data analysis

ENSECOL211.name: The Science of Evolution
ENSECOL211.contribution: examines selection, genetic variation, adaptation, phylogeny and evolutionary history, including a species project using Tinbergen’s four questions

GOSPHIL214.name: Philosophy of Mind
GOSPHIL214.contribution: examines mind, consciousness, identity, physicalism and neuropsychological cases through philosophical argument, complementing empirical neuroscience

GOSPHIL313.name: Free Will, Time & the Self
GOSPHIL313.contribution: examines free will, agency, determinism, addiction and scientific challenges to responsibility as conceptual complements to behavioural explanation

HCBBIOM111.name: Epidemiology & Public Health
HCBBIOM111.contribution: develops epidemiological design, bias, confounding and causality for studying disease patterns and evaluating biomedical evidence

HCBBIOM211.name: Functional Anatomy
HCBBIOM211.contribution: examines human organ-system anatomy and functional spatial relationships through anatomical images and practical observation, supporting brain-body study

HCBBIOM311.name: Pharmacology
HCBBIOM311.contribution: examines drug action, kinetics, metabolism, toxicity and pharmacogenomics, including nervous-system drugs and a psychoactive-drug research proposal

HCBBIOM312.name: Infection & Immunity
HCBBIOM312.contribution: examines innate and adaptive immune mechanisms, host–microbe interactions and disease, including flow-cytometry analysis and research synthesis

HCBBIOM313.name: Mechanisms of Disease
HCBBIOM313.contribution: connects normal organ function and regulation to endocrine, nervous-system and other disease mechanisms through clinical-case and pathophysiological analysis

HCBCOGN112.name: Neurobiology
HCBCOGN112.contribution: examines comparative neuroanatomy, neurophysiology, animal behaviour, rhythms, sleep and mood/eating disorders, including laboratory introductions and animal-research ethics

HCBCOGN212.name: Perception & Action
HCBCOGN212.contribution: examines neural mechanisms of sensory information processing and goal-directed action using cognitive-neuroscience and neuropsychological approaches

HCBCOGN311.name: Higher Order Functions
HCBCOGN311.contribution: examines attention, memory, emotion, cognitive control and consciousness in relation to neural function and dysfunction, with an attentional-blink experiment and research proposal

HCBCOGN312.name: Psycholinguistics
HCBCOGN312.contribution: examines neural and psychological mechanisms of language acquisition, comprehension and production, including impairments and experimental approaches

HCBGATE101.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
HCBGATE101.contribution: introduces cells, biomolecules, energy metabolism, DNA, heredity and gene expression as biological foundations for neuroscience

HCBGATE102.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
HCBGATE102.contribution: introduces neural signalling, brain anatomy, development, learning and behavioural/neuroscience research approaches as foundations for brain-behaviour study

HCBLIFE211.name: Molecular Cell Biology
HCBLIFE211.contribution: examines cell regulation, gene expression, membranes, trafficking and signalling, including primary-literature analysis of a drug target

HCBLIFE212.name: Human Physiology
HCBLIFE212.contribution: examines homeostasis, neuroendocrine signalling and integrated human organ-system regulation, supporting biological explanations of brain-body interaction

HCBLIFE213.name: Biochemistry
HCBLIFE213.contribution: examines biomolecular structure, enzyme kinetics and metabolic pathways, linking biochemical defects to disease mechanisms

HCBLIFE214.name: Life Science Laboratory
HCBLIFE214.contribution: develops practical molecular, biochemical and microbiological techniques through protein purification, transformation, DNA analysis and reproducible laboratory reports

HCBLIFE311.name: Molecular Pathology & Genetics
HCBLIFE311.contribution: examines genetic and cellular disease mechanisms, inheritance, variation, epigenetics and molecular diagnosis, with a controlled research-grant proposal and ethics debate

HCBPSYC111.name: Social Psychology
HCBPSYC111.contribution: examines social cognition, influence, group processes and behaviour through empirical research and a study proposal, providing a psychological context for cognitive neuroscience

HCBPSYC211.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
HCBPSYC211.contribution: develops experimental design and applied multivariable statistical models in health and behavioural research using data-analysis papers and a poster

HCBPSYC212.name: Psychopathology
HCBPSYC212.contribution: examines mental disorder through biological, psychological, social and cultural explanations, with case analysis and a structured literature study

HCBPSYC311.name: Medical & Health Psychology
HCBPSYC311.contribution: examines stress, illness, symptoms and health behaviour through biological, psychological and social interactions, supporting the brain-body and mental-health strand

HCBPSYC313.name: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics
HCBPSYC313.contribution: develops systematic review and meta-analysis, effect sizes, heterogeneity, bias and research reporting in behavioural and medical inquiry

HCBPSYC314.name: Lifespan Developmental Psychology
HCBPSYC314.contribution: examines physical, cognitive, social and emotional development across the lifespan, including biological/environmental influences and a life-story study

alignment.rationale: Both develop scholarly reading, academic writing, research questions, reflection and presentation. UvA specifically embeds these skills in psychobiological reporting.
Both develop research design, measurement, estimation, statistical testing and regression, with data analysis in R. UCR also includes a student research project.
Both develop programming in Python and implementation of executable tasks. UvA specifically programmes a visual-search experiment; UCR provides broader programming foundations.
Both develop scientific functions, calculus, complex numbers and differential-equation modelling as quantitative foundations.

Both examine evolutionary explanations of adaptation and behaviour, including natural selection, reproduction and Tinbergen’s questions. UvA concentrates more specifically on cognition and behavioural ecology.
Both examine consciousness, mind-body relations, reductionism and interpretations of neuroscience. UvA additionally provides a general cognitive-psychology introduction.
Both examine nervous-system anatomy and physiology in relation to behaviour. UvA also includes detailed membrane electrophysiology and peripheral organ-system anatomy and physiology.
Both examine sensory processing, visual perception and mechanisms linking perception to action. UvA also gives explicit attention to consciousness.
Both examine memory and higher cognitive functions through brain systems and experimental evidence. UvA extends much further into cellular mechanisms of learning and memory.
Both introduce neural organisation, biological and psychological processes, and relationships between brain function and behaviour.
Both examine molecular cell structure, bioenergetics, protein handling, membranes, trafficking and cell communication. UvA includes an integrated experimental practical.
Both develop hands-on molecular and biochemical laboratory skills, DNA/protein analysis and reproducible experimental reporting. UvA uses a specific glucocorticoid-receptor experiment.

Both examine inheritance, genetic variation, gene regulation and molecular mechanisms. UCR concentrates on human genetic disease; UvA also gives substantial coverage to population genetics and evolution.
Both develop multivariable statistical analysis, model choice and reasoned interpretation of behavioural evidence. UvA integrates this with philosophy of science and Bayesian reasoning.

Both develop substantial literature research, critical synthesis and scientific communication. UCR specialises in systematic review and quantitative meta-analysis; UvA’s review is a topic-based literature study.
Both examine cognitive and social development and biological/environmental influences. UvA additionally gives substantial coverage to embryonic development and molecular neurodevelopment.
Academic writing and research skills are represented elsewhere; no second course is counted as the separate continuation of the dedicated skills sequence.
Personal development is represented in the first-year skills placement; no additional course is counted as a separate study/career-orientation trajectory.

Selected courses develop experimental design and cognitive experiments, but their strongest primary placements are methods and cognitive functions; none is counted again as this dedicated student-run experimental-psychology practical.
Introductory neuroscience includes measurement perspectives, but no selected UCR course provides a dedicated EEG acquisition, analysis and reporting practical.
Ethics is considered in several selected courses, but none is a dedicated practical bioethics course across the scope of this component.
Selected laboratory and neurobiology courses provide complementary skills; none provides this dedicated combination of channel modelling and hands-on electrophysiological experiments.

Neurobiology, physiology and cognition address aspects of emotional and internal regulation elsewhere. No additional course is counted for this integrated emotion, reward, motivation and neurohormonal sequence.
Open elective space remains unspecified; no individual course, minor or exchange host is invented.
No compulsory 30-EC psychobiological research internship is scheduled at UCR. Optional independent research is displayed separately outside scheduled credits.
